methods.name: SetVariation
methods.description: Penrose's "variation": the same string, the same picture. Any text folds to a seed; a number is used as it is. SeedRandom refuses a seed at or above 1,999,999,999, so the fold stays under it.

methods.name: SolveProfile
methods.description: the live figure (DN8g) -------------------------------------------------- A RE-SOLVE FROM WHERE THE FIGURE STANDS. Nothing is recompiled and no start is drawn: the current values are the start, and the solver settles the picture nearby. LayoutMs() then reports this solve. where the last solve spent its time, in ms: building the energy text, compiling it, minimising, reading the violations, and folding derived names to numbers (counted inside :text) -- plus the rounds

methods.name: Relayout
methods.description: Same as Layout: the answer

methods.name: DragTo
methods.description: THE DRAG. The shape's centre is put where the author released it, held there while the rest of the figure re-solves around it, and let go again unless it was pinned before. A shape whose centre no rule left free -- a placed name, a square derived from its triangle -- is refused: there is nothing there to drag.

methods.name: Pin
methods.description: A PIN holds every free property of a shape at its current value through any re-solve, cold or warm -- the plastic editor's pin, for a figure whose coordinates are solved rather than laid out.

methods.name: Pins
methods.description: the shapes pinned, by path

methods.name: Draggable
methods.description: the shapes a gesture can take hold of: a free centre, and a body

methods.name: PickAt
methods.description: WHAT IS UNDER THE POINTER: the nearest draggable shape whose body -- or a ten-pixel reach around its centre -- holds the point; "" when the pointer is on the paper.

methods.name: OnPress
methods.description: THE GESTURE, in the plastic editor's three verbs. A press takes hold of what is under the pointer; a move previews and re-solves NOTHING -- the window paints the dragged shape where DragPreview() says -- and the release is the one drag, from where the author let go.

methods.description: The solved geometry of one shape: [ :kind, :cx, :cy, :r ] for a circle, [ :kind, :cx, :cy, :w, :h ] for a rect or text, [ :kind, :x1, :y1, :x2, :y2 ] for a line.

methods.name: ValueOf
methods.description: The solved value of any name: an unknown, a constant, a field, a derived property -- "u.arrow.x2", "U.ox".

methods.name: DrawIndexOf
methods.description: Where a shape falls in the drawing order: 1 is painted first and so sits at the back. A shape that must not be buried has to come out with a HIGHER index than everything that could cover it, and that is a fact about the picture worth asserting rather than eyeballing -- layering is a partial order, and the depths it relaxes to are not obvious from reading the rules.

methods.name: PolygonOf
methods.description: A polygon's vertices, or a spline's control points, in order: [ x1, y1, x2, y2, ... ].

methods.name: SplinePointsOf
methods.description: The polyline a spline is drawn as, in px -- the control points are in PolygonOf. CATMULL-ROM, CENTRIPETAL: for each span P1-P2 the four points P0..P3 are blended with knots spaced by the square root of the chord, which is the parametrisation that never cusps or loops between two points however they are spaced (Yuksel, Schaefer, Keyser 2011). An open spline doubles its end points so the curve reaches them; a closed one wraps. Twelve samples per span.

methods.name: CurvePointsOf
methods.description: The polyline a geodesic is drawn as: [ x1, y1, x2, y2, ... ] in px.

methods.name: MarkStrokesOf
methods.description: The strokes a mark is drawn as: a list of polylines, each flat in px.

methods.name: ToCanvas
methods.description: drawing

methods.name: Rendition
methods.description: A VALUE THAT SAYS WHAT IT IS (DN9g) --------------------------------- A picture's natural rendition is its drawn geometry, which travels as text and needs no file. The raster and the substance's graph are the same picture seen the other two ways a consumer asked for.

methods.name: RenditionAtQ
methods.description: Same as RenditionAsXT: An empty path means the name this class would have chosen, so every caller written before today means exactly what it meant. A path given for a CARRIED kind is refused by name rather than ignored: a caller who asks for an SVG at a path is not asking for nothing, they are holding a wrong belief about the contract, and being told is the cheaper outcome.

methods.name: Fact
methods.description: THE GENERAL KIND IS :expr, and the others are its named shortcuts. A picture already has a language for talking about itself -- the one a Style writes its rules in -- so a fact asks a question in that language and the answer comes off the same tape the solver used. That is what makes a caption's number the picture's number rather than a second calculation that could drift from it.

methods.name: ConstraintText
methods.description: the energy text of a rule, so a narration can show what the engine was handed and how big it became

methods.name: SetPictureTheme
methods.description: WHAT A FRAME MAY CHANGE BETWEEN TWO PICTURES (DN9f). Haro copies an object on assignment, so a caller holding the substance or the style is holding a different one from the picture's; these are the doors through which a narration's action reaches the picture it is about.

methods.name: SetSubstanceData
methods.description: A DATUM IS CONTENT, so changing one means the picture is compiled again -- unlike a theme, which changes only what a role resolves to.

methods.name: SetWindow
methods.description: WHAT DOES NOT SCALE IS THE TYPE. A zoom here is for reading, not a photographic enlargement: the names keep their size and only their positions move, so a close view is more legible rather than merely bigger. Stroke widths do scale, because a hairline blown up eight times and still one pixel wide reads as a different picture.

methods.name: WindowOn
methods.description: centred on what a frame is about, with a reach around it -- the form an author actually writes

methods.name: WindowScale
methods.description: how much bigger the view is than the figure; 1 with no window

methods.name: IsInWindow
methods.description: IS THIS THING IN VIEW? What a frame shows decides whether a mark is any use, and a mark pointing at something outside the window is a narration defect the one gate reports.

methods.name: VisibleShapes
methods.description: the shapes a reader can actually see, in draw order

methods.name: Emphasis
methods.description: EVERY MARK IS DERIVED, NEVER PLACED. Its geometry comes from the picture's solved values or from a rule actually in force -- which is the whole point of the plane, because a mark a person positions is a mark nobody checks. Marks are minted AFTER the solve and hold every existing unknown pinned while they place themselves, so adding one cannot move the figure it describes: frame two's figure is frame one's figure, to the last pixel. A HARO, A FOCUS OR A DIM. Emphasis changes how a shape already in the picture reads, so it mints nothing for :focus and :dim -- it rewrites the shape's own stroke -- and mints one circle for :ring.

methods.name: Measure
methods.description: A DIMENSION BETWEEN TWO THINGS, WITH ITS NUMBER. The line runs centre to centre, the number is the distance FACT -- so the figure and the caption cannot disagree -- and the number's own label is solved off the ink like any other name.

methods.name: Callout
methods.description: A SENTENCE ATTACHED TO A THING. The sentence may carry a hole, and a hole is filled from a FACT rather than typed -- which is the rule the whole plane exists to enforce. The label is solved: off the ink, off other names, on the paper, exactly as a vertex's name is, which is why a callout needed no new solver.

methods.name: Show
methods.description: A RULE'S OWN BOUNDARY, AS A SHAPE. The leash a name must stay inside is a circle nobody ever drew, because it exists only as a term in the energy; showing it is reading that term's own arguments and turning them into geometry. Only the forms whose boundary IS a shape are shown, and the rest are refused by name rather than approximated.

methods.name: Region
methods.description: AN AREA, TINTED. Where Show draws a boundary, Region fills what the boundary encloses -- the strip an edge forbids, the disc a clearance reserves. A strip is the segment's own rectangle, four corners derived from the segment's direction, so it bends with the picture.

methods.name: Marks
methods.description: what this picture carries, as [ path, kind ] -- so a frame can say what it added and a later frame can take it away again

methods.name: FillOf
methods.description: The colour a shape is drawn with, after its rule is resolved: what the guard reads, and what a consumer of the SVG gets.

methods.name: StrokeOf
methods.description: Same as Layout: the answer

methods.name: Background
methods.description: the paper's colour: the theme's background

methods.name: MatchCandidates
methods.description: how many candidate bindings the last compile enumerated

methods.name: StartsTried
methods.description: Uniform over the canvas, as Penrose samples; radii and sizes from a band that gives the solver room. Three draws, the one with the least initial energy kept -- Penrose 4.2.1. How many starts the last layout needed, and which one it kept. A start the graph could not give -- a planar one on a tree, a layout on a substance with no graph -- falls back to random and says so.

methods.name: AdvisoryUnmet
methods.description: Crossing rules left unmet when the start was not planar and the rule was therefore advice: zero for a planar start, and for any picture that has no crossing rule.

methods.name: StartUsed
methods.description: Same as Layout: the answer

methods.name: StartedPlanar
methods.description: Did the last layout begin from a planar embedding? False when the style asked for none, and false when it asked and the graph could not give one -- a tree, a path, anything Tutte collapses.

methods.name: OuterFace
methods.description: The face the planar start was built on, as object names in cycle order; empty when there was no planar start.

methods.name: Ink
methods.description: Every drawn stroke as a segment, [ x1, y1, x2, y2, cOwner, cPath ] -- what a rule that judges the picture reads, once per solve

methods.name: Texts
methods.description: EVERY DRAWN NAME -- the text shapes that are visible and say something -- once per solve, like the ink. Every name rule's scope listed them by resolving every shape of the picture, and the governance asks a scope thousands of times: on the five-thousand-dot picture that was five thousand resolutions per ask.

methods.name: AddType
methods.description: types

methods.name: AddSubtype
methods.description: "Hydrogen <: Atom": wherever an Atom is expected, a Hydrogen matches.

methods.name: TypeMatches
methods.description: TRUE when an object of pcActual may stand where pcWanted is asked for -- the same type, or a subtype of it, at any depth.

methods.name: AddPredicate
methods.description: predicates

methods.name: AddSymmetricPredicate
methods.description: Symmetric: Disjoint(A, B) IS Disjoint(B, A). Penrose restricts this to binary predicates over one type, and so does this.

methods.name: AddFunction
methods.description: functions and constructors

methods.name: AddConstructor
methods.description: a constructor is a function whose name is its output type

methods.name: Kind
methods.description: what it is

methods.name: Diagram
methods.description: the solved picture itself: an stzMathDiagram, with everything one can answer -- ShapeOf, Fact, Violations, the renditions. IT IS A COPY: Haro copies an object a method returns, so a theme or a datum set on it never reaches the figure's own picture. Set the theme and the data THROUGH the figure (SetTheme, SetDatum); found 2026-09-26 when 32 catalogue pictures rendered "dark" came out byte-identical to light.

methods.name: SetTheme
methods.description: the theme, on the figure's OWN picture: no second solve, a theme changes only what every role resolves to

methods.name: Layout
methods.description: the solve

methods.name: Why
methods.description: what was computed and what was solved, in one sentence each: the computed half is the domain file's sentence, the solved half the diagram's own

methods.name: RunCount
methods.description: the polylines drawn: a piece longer than 64 samples is several runs

methods.name: Window
methods.description: the window in the author's units: [ xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax ]

methods.name: Marks
methods.description: every mark as [ kind, x, y ] -- "zero", "extremum" or "given"

methods.name: SetDatum
methods.description: the live figure, and a datum changed in place ------------------------- HARO HANDS BACK A COPY when a method returns an object, so anything that must change THIS figure's picture goes through here, never through Diagram() -- a witness that tampered a copy found nothing.

methods.name: Pin
methods.description: a shape whose centre a rule left free is pinned or dragged by the diagram's own gesture; a NOTE is not such a shape -- see MoveNoteTo

methods.name: MoveNoteTo
methods.description: A NOTE IS MOVED BY ITS OFFSETS. Its place is derived from its mark plus two unknowns, n.ox and n.oy (the free side is the mark's datum), which is what lets every note start inside its leash; a drag by shape (DragTo) wants a free centre and refuses it. This writes the two slots, holds them, and re-solves the rest of the figure around them.

methods.name: Text
methods.description: THE TEXT RENDITION a box plot carries (the Tukey plan's TK3): the five numbers and the box in characters, for a terminal or a test log

methods.name: ToSVG
methods.description: the renditions

methods.name: ValueAt
methods.description: the value alone -- no tape walk, which is what a line search wants

methods.name: GradientAt
methods.description: the gradient: one entry per variable, in the order they were named

methods.name: ValueAndGradientAt
methods.description: value and gradient together, because the backward pass computes both and asking for them separately evaluates the expression twice

methods.name: DerivativeAt
methods.description: the partial derivative with respect to one named variable

methods.name: Param
methods.description: the parameters ---------------------------------------------------------- a slider: a name the declaration mentions as {name}, its range, and where it stands now (the range's start when not said)

methods.name: Set
methods.description: MOVE A SLIDER: clamped to its range; the computed half follows on the next frame, the solved half on the next Settle

methods.name: Resolved
methods.description: the solved half: the figure where the parameters last settled ---------- the declaration with every {name} replaced by its value

methods.name: Settle
methods.description: REBUILD AND RE-SOLVE the figure for the parameters as they stand now, and keep what it cost -- the solved half's number

methods.name: Figure
methods.description: the settled figure -- settled first if it never was

methods.name: LiveCurve
methods.description: the live samples of the curve on the settled figure's window, as pixel pieces: [ [ x1, y1, x2, y2, ... ], ... ], broken where the function leaves the window or is not finite

methods.name: LiveSamples
methods.description: the live samples in the author's units, for a check: [ [ x, y ], ... ]

methods.name: DrawLiveOn
methods.description: THE LIVE CURVE DRAWN INTO A CANVAS, cleared first: the overlay the window draws over the settled picture. Keeps what it cost.

methods.name: Counts
methods.description: the counts a gate asserts the frame's structure by: settles, tape calls and flushes since the motion was made

methods.name: Frame
methods.description: a frame, offscreen: the same composition the window shows -------------- a fresh canvas with the settled picture and the live curve on it; the caller frees it. The overlay path of the window draws the two as separate layers; here they are one canvas, since a saved frame is one picture.

methods.name: Play
methods.description: the window loop ---------------------------------------------------------- THE PLAYER: the settled picture retained in one canvas, the live curve redrawn each frame in an overlay; the first parameter on left/right, the second on up/down, a hundredth of its range per frame held; the picture settles when no key is held and something moved. Escape closes.

methods.name: State
methods.description: declared STATES ---------------------------------------------------------- A STATE is a caption and the acts that reach it from the state before. An act is a list led by its verb: [ :DragTo,   "A.icon", x, y ]      a free shape to a place [ :DragBy,   "A.icon", dx, dy ]    the same, from where it stands [ :SetData,  "fr", "ymax", 2 ]     a datum into the substance [ :SetTheme, "dark" ]              the picture's theme [ :Set,      "a", 2 ]              a parameter (a :Function motion) A state with no act is the picture as it stands -- the opening frame.

methods.name: StateFact
methods.description: a fact the caption of the LAST declared state shows as {hole}: bound now, computed when the frame is closed, on the picture at that state

methods.name: Picture
methods.description: the picture as it stands: the motion's own copy for a :Diagram, the settled figure's diagram for a :Function -- a copy, for reading

methods.name: Apply
methods.description: THE LIVE PASS: the acts of one state, on the motion's own picture. States are steps, so state n is reached from state n-1; a caller that jumps is asking for the acts of n from wherever the picture stands, which is what it gets and what Applied() then says.

methods.name: ExportTo
methods.description: the export: a storyboard driven by the same acts ------------------------ EVERY STATE A FRAME. The storyboard takes its own copy of the picture from where it stands now, replays each state's acts on that copy through its own Act (so the frame it closes is the picture AFTER the acts), binds each fact to be computed on that frame, writes the frame as a PNG in the folio, and the narration beside them. A :Function motion settles per state and hands each settled figure in as a frame; its parameters are put back afterwards, so the export leaves the motion where it found it in both cases.

methods.name: PlayStates
methods.description: the player of states ------------------------------------------------------ each state applied and held on the window for pnDwellMs; Right or Space advance early, Escape closes; the last state holds until Escape. A :Function motion drawn live composes its frame, any other draws its picture as it stands.

methods.name: ForAll
methods.description: ForAll("Set x", rows) -- rows are DATA. Each row is one of: [ :shape,     "x.icon", :circle | :rect | :text | :line | :curve | :poly | :mark, [ props ] ] [ :delete,    "x.icon" ]              unmint a shape an earlier rule made [ :unknown,   "p.sx", lo, hi ]        a variable the solver owns [ :field,     "U.ox", number | "expression" ] [ :override,  "u.arrow.x2", number | "expression" ] [ :ensure,    "fn", [ args ] ]        a constraint [ :encourage, "fn", [ args ] ]        an objective [ :layer,     "x.text", :above | :below, "x.icon" ] A property or argument is a number, a path ("x.icon.r"), or an expression over paths ("U.ox + 14*ux(u.arrow)").

methods.name: StartPlanar
methods.description: A PLANAR START. The solver never leaves the basin it starts in -- DN7f measured 84 crossing terms holding 10,138 energy units at convergence that no weight could spend -- so the start is where planarity is decided. A style that draws a graph declares which objects are its vertices, which shape's centre carries them, and which constructors are its edges; the diagram then seeds those centres by Tutte's embedding rather than at random. Everything else in the picture still starts where it always did.

methods.name: StartLayout
methods.description: LAYOUTS AS STARTS (DN8b). The graph plane's own engines -- hierarchical, ring, force, mesh, sequence -- computed on the graph the substance's vertices and edges make, and overlaid as the solver's start. The planar start is one of them. StartTrying names SEVERAL: the solver takes them in order, and the first that ends lawful is the picture -- so the seed is no longer what decides whether a lattice crosses.

methods.name: Starts
methods.description: the starts to try, in order; empty means one random start

methods.name: SetMargin
methods.description: A MARGIN inside the paper. The on-canvas rule holds every shape inside the canvas exactly, and a style whose vertices repel one another pushes them onto that line: the dodecahedron came out with its outer face touching all four edges. A margin moves the line in.

methods.name: SetTheme
methods.description: COLOUR AS MEANING (DN8d). A style writes ROLES -- :primary for the one accent, :neutral for ink, :muted for secondary ink, :background for the paper -- and the theme decides what each is. A theme is named here; the diagram resolves every role through it at draw time, and a text with no colour of its own takes the best of black and white on what it sits on, measured. Content colours -- Byrne's plate, the quaternion table's eight -- stay the style's own data.

methods.name: SolveLabelsAfter
methods.description: LABELS AFTER SHAPES. The joint first stage lets a name's constraints move the shapes -- which an Euler diagram needs, since a set must be large enough for its name, and which a graph must NOT have: a name held off an edge pulls on the edge's endpoints, and at a high penalty weight eight names threw a planar cube away to make room for themselves. Under this, the first stage sees no label term at all, and the names find their room against frozen shapes.

A table is different -- a cell IS its row, its column and its value -- and a heatmap is nothing but numbers. SetData puts one on an object under a key; any Style expression reads it as "x.key", to drive a position or, through a colour rule, a fill.

In all those spots the word must stay a literal -- resolution would corrupt the program.

methods.name: GlyphOf
methods.description: The kind's glyph: the geometric shape the renderer draws. The DEFAULT profile answers through the SAME shared table both faces already read (StzNodeShapeForType), so expressing the diagram as a profile moves no pixel -- DN0's whole claim. A declared kind outranks the table; an unknown kind in an OPEN profile falls back to it; in a CLOSED one it answers "", and the renderer's existing fallback (a box) still draws while Check() reports the finding.

methods.name: Forbid
methods.description: RULES

methods.name: ForbidFor
methods.description: A rule a KIND carries -- DN2. :Inbound forbidden for an initial pseudostate means nothing may transition INTO it; :Outbound for a final state means nothing leaves. The kind is the subject because that is how the domain speaks: "a final state has no exits" is a statement about final states, not about any edge.

methods.name: MayLink
methods.description: Takes the DIAGRAM because two of the primitives are about the graph the link would join, not about the link alone (DN1, org charts): a second parent is only a second parent given the edges that exist, and a cycle is only a cycle given the paths that do.

methods.name: Check

methods.name: SetRankDir
methods.description: GRAMMAR

methods.name: SetEdgesDirected
methods.description: Declared by the profile, so it is one line in a domain rather than a special case in the drawer, and it is not electric-only: a UML association and a communication link are undirected for the same reason.

methods.name: SetOneInk
methods.description: A SCHEMATIC HAS NO SUCH DIVISION. The outline of a resistor and the wire joined to it are one conductor drawing, and two inks there state a difference that does not exist -- the wires read as thinner and lighter than the parts, which is what the Principal saw. A profile whose edges ARE part of the same object as its nodes says so here, and the diagram then draws both in the node ink.

methods.name: SetNameInside
methods.description: Declared per kind, because it is a claim about how the DOMAIN draws that glyph, not about the glyph everywhere.

methods.name: AddCompartmentKey
methods.description: Same fault as the four layout modes and the one shape named "diamond", and this is the third time in a week: a rule whose membership is enumerated stops being applied the moment something new arrives. A notation says what its own compartments are; the default is UML's pair, so nothing that existed before this changes.

methods.name: SetNameOutside
methods.description: THE OPPOSITE DECLARATION: a kind whose inside is spoken for. The renderer writes a name inside any glyph big enough to hold it, which is right until the glyph holds something else -- a Petri place holds its tokens, and "Key" written over one dot read as "K.y". Declared per kind, so a notation says it once.

methods.name: SetPeerChildren
methods.description: A PARENT'S CHILDREN ARE PEERS. The layout gives a parent's column to the child that carries the longest continuation -- right for a flow, where the graph itself says "this way onward". A fault tree's gate has inputs, not a continuation: none of them is the line onward, so the gate stands at their middle whatever hangs beneath each. Declared by the notation, read by the layout.

methods.name: IsExact
methods.description: Numeric surprise is almost always about a frame the caller could not see: a rounding, a binary-float representation, a division that does not terminate. So the number carries that fact rather than making you deduce it -- the same habit as the natural layer's evidential register.

methods.name: MathFunctionQ
methods.description: NOT `Function()`: Haro accepts `function` as a synonym for `func`, so a method by that name is a C6 "Error in function name" at load time. Same family as naming a variable `oR`, which folds onto the `or` keyword. an OBJECT accessor, so it is Q-only -- a plain twin would return an object, which is exactly what the plain form must never do

methods.name: MinimizeFrom
methods.description: THE ANSWER IS A RECORD, NOT A POINT, for the same reason the hypothesis tests return one: a bare answer cannot tell you it did not converge. :status says how it stopped, :evaluations is the honest cost (an iteration that line-searched twelve times is not one unit of work), and :why says it in words.

methods.name: MaximizeFrom
methods.description: THE LARGEST value, by minimising the negative. Doing it here rather than telling you to rewrite the expression is the point: -f has the same maximiser as f has minimiser, but the VALUE comes back negated, and forgetting to flip it back is the obvious way to get this wrong.

Adding two instructions aimed at the observed failures -- "do not explain the structure", and "replace every <...> with a real value" -- took it to 0/10: a small model told not to explain explained more, and the negation was the thing it echoed. It answered 0 for as long as that was true; gbnf_machine.zig is the rung underneath it, so it answers 1 since 2026-08-20 -- the ENGINE is the authority on that number, never this comment.

methods.name: Center
methods.description: THE NAME FORM CARRIES THE SEMANTICS, which is a Softanza law rather than a style: an ACTIVE verb -- Standardize(), Center() -- DOES the thing and returns nothing; the PASSIVE form -- Standardized(), Centered() -- returns the transformed DATA and leaves the object alone; and the Q twin does the thing and returns the object so calls chain. The first version of this class had Standardized() mutating the analysis and returning This, which got both halves wrong at once: a passive name for an active act, and a plain method returning an object where plain methods return data. CENTER each feature on its mean and leave the units alone -- covariance PCA. The features that vary most, in their own units, dominate.

methods.name: Standardize
methods.description: CENTER and then divide each feature by its standard deviation -- correlation PCA. Every feature counts equally, whatever it was measured in.

methods.name: Centered
methods.description: ── and the passive forms, which return the prepared DATA ── The data centered on the column means, original untouched. This is what a covariance PCA actually decomposes, so it is worth being able to look at.

methods.name: Standardized
methods.description: The data centered AND divided by the column standard deviations. What a correlation PCA decomposes.

methods.name: UseSampleVariance
methods.description: ── the variance convention, from the library's one authority ──

methods.name: Components
methods.description: The sign is fixed by convention (the largest loading of each component is made positive) because a direction has no preferred sign -- v and -v are the same axis explaining the same variance -- and without a convention two runs can look like they disagree.

methods.name: Loadings
methods.description: Same as Components: The sign is fixed by convention (the largest loading of each component is made positive) because a direction has no preferred sign -- v and -v are the same axis explaining the same variance -- and without a convention two runs can look like they disagree.

methods.name: Scores
methods.description: The data in component coordinates: row i is sample i, column j its position along component j. Centered by construction, so each column averages zero.

methods.name: ExplainedVariance
methods.description: How much variance each component accounts for, in the units of the prepared data. These SUM to TotalVariance() -- the decomposition redistributes the variance and cannot create or destroy any.

methods.name: ExplainedVarianceRatio
methods.description: The same, as fractions of the total. This is the number people quote.

methods.name: NumberOfComponentsFor
methods.description: How many components to keep to retain a given fraction of the variance -- the usual way the number of components is chosen.

methods.name: Mean
methods.description: The centering that was applied, kept because projecting NEW data needs exactly the same one. Data centered on its own mean lands in a different space.

methods.name: Inverse
methods.description: That identity is checked in the guard, and it is a far stronger statement than any reconstruction number the learned inverses can offer. It says the arithmetic is RIGHT, where they can only say the result looked plausible.

methods.name: Reconstructed
methods.description: the training rows put through Transform() and back again -- what the analysis retained of the data it was given, which is the picture worth looking at when deciding how many components are enough

methods.name: Counters
methods.description: The last two are G2's, and they are the phase's own gauge. G0 measured 988 GetStringWidth calls per re-layout, unmemoized by RmlUi; at ~1 us per real shape that is ~1 ms/frame before a glyph is drawn, so the plan made a width cache a PRECONDITION. widthCalls is what RmlUi asked for and shapeCalls is what actually reached the shaper -- the gap between them is the cache doing its job, and if they ever converge the precondition has silently lapsed.

methods.name: TextMeshes
methods.description: That is not hypothetical: registering one font family twice used to free the id the existing faces pointed at, so widths came back -1, the quads were zero-wide, RmlUi culled them, and whichever panel had been built first lost its text. Two panels sharing a font is all it took, and every single-panel guard stayed green. The invariant lives here now so the next such bug is a failing number, not a screenshot.

methods.name: TextIsWhole
methods.description: TRUE when every generated string became geometry.

methods.name: UseFont
methods.description: Answers an stzFont for the caller to paint with, or NULL on refusal.

methods.description: The stzFont this panel paints a recorded command with. Matching is by the engine font id the command carries -- not by family name, which a fallback may have changed under us.

methods.name: PointerMovedTo
methods.description: EVENTS ARE DRAINED, NEVER DISPATCHED. RmlUi routes and bubbles, the engine writes down what arrived, and Events() hands over the list. A callback per event would re-enter Haro from inside a C++ dispatch, which is not safe, and the house has already settled this shape twice: the display list and the text commands.

methods.name: ClickAt
methods.description: The whole gesture, because a click is a press AND a release and a caller that forgets the second one gets a button stuck down.

methods.name: ElementAt
methods.description: The element under a point, by name. "" when the point hits nothing that carries a name -- a fair answer, not a failure.

methods.name: FromWindow
methods.description: the conversions, named at the boundary ------------------------------ A window's pixels are the panel's when the panel fills the window, which is the case stzWindow.Draw arranges. Named anyway: the reader of a frame loop should see WHERE the space changes.

methods.name: FromTexture
methods.description: A panel hanging in a 3D scene is hit by a RAY, and what the caller has after the intersection is a texture coordinate. This is the whole of the in-scene input mapping (§6's tier): uv in, panel pixels out. v is flipped because a texture's origin is bottom-left and a panel's is top-left -- the one place that difference is stated, so no caller has to remember it.

methods.name: SetTextOf
methods.description: The difference is measurable, and the guard measures it: after a rebuild every string is generated again; after a set, only the ones that actually changed are. GenerateCalls() reports both. One element's words. The value is DATA -- it is escaped at the seam, so a model holding "<span>" cannot inject markup into a document the court already passed.

methods.name: SetStyleOf
methods.description: An EMPTY value removes the property, handing the element back to the stylesheet. Without that, a binding that had fired once could never be undone.

methods.name: FocusOn
methods.description: Rule 80 (Keyboard Sovereignty) is `machine` tier, so this is legally required rather than polish. RmlUi owns the traversal -- tab order in document order, and a spatial heuristic for directional moves -- and what is added here is the QUERY and the COUNTED refusal.

methods.name: Focused
methods.description: The focused element's name, or "" when nothing is focused.

methods.name: FocusNext
methods.description: TRUE when focus MOVED. A refusal at the end of a ring is a real answer, not an error, so it answers FALSE rather than raising.

methods.name: FocusUp
methods.description: Directional moves, for an arrow key or a gamepad stick. RmlUi picks the target by a spatial heuristic, which is what the WAI-ARIA APG contract wants inside a composite widget.

methods.name: TabRing
methods.description: A ring is a CYCLE, and this enters it wherever focus currently sits: RmlUi resumes tabbing from the last focused element even after a blur, so calling this with `cancel` focused answers the same cycle rotated. The SET and the ORDER are stable; the entry point is not. Call it before touching focus if the first stop matters -- as the guard does.

methods.name: Events
methods.description: The SOURCE is the frame §7 chose to surface, and it earns its place: Rule 80 makes "reachable by a human keyboard" materially different from "something dispatched a click", and G4 needs an assistive activation distinguishable from a pointer one.

methods.name: EventsDropped
methods.description: What the bounded queue threw away. A caller that stops draining stops receiving, and this is how it finds out.

methods.name: EventsFor
methods.description: Every event whose target is one named element.

methods.name: Texts
methods.description: Text crosses as COMMANDS, not as quads. RmlUi asked our font engine for the string; the engine recorded the request instead of rasterizing it, and the canvas draws it with the same shaper. That is why this plane owns no glyph atlas and no second rasterizer.

methods.name: BoxOf
methods.description: The laid-out box of one element: [x, y, w, h], in panel pixels. Empty when there is no such element -- an absence, not a raise, since asking about an element that may not exist is a fair question.

methods.name: DrawInto
methods.description: output -------------------------------------------------------------- Put the panel's triangles into a canvas. The canvas decides what happens next -- ToSVG() with no device, ToPNG() with one, a window, or a texture mapped onto a quad in a 3D scene. The panel does not know and must not care.

methods.name: ToCanvas

methods.name: SetProfile
methods.description: A stzPlatformProfile DESCRIBES the solution -- its constituents (a server, a superapp, an app, ...) and their target systems. The platform OWNS one and drives its lifecycle: Build() the platform and its constituents, THEN Deploy() them -- two separate, ordered operations. (SetProfile snapshots the profile, so configure it fully first -- the aliasing doctrine.)

methods.name: Build

methods.name: Deploy
methods.description: DEPLOY the built parts to their target systems. Refuses if the platform was not built first -- Build() and Deploy() are separate. For each part, the deploy-time LOWERING bridge turns its rehearsed (up-enable) feature ops into a real target ARTIFACT (firmware source for an MCU, a manifest otherwise) -- the flash/upload of that artifact to the device is the one remaining external step.

methods.name: SetWorld
methods.description: == 1. GENERATION ======================================================== SET the world this platform envelopes -- by HARVESTING its declarations into the platform's own records, right now. It does NOT hold the world: Haro copies an object into an attribute, so a held stzApp would be a dead snapshot the moment the caller touched it (see the aliasing note in the header). Call this AFTER the world is declared. The world is ASKED through its own accessors -- a platform never reaches into another object's attributes. (A constellation ADDs many worlds; a platform SETs its one.)

methods.description: Past degree four no formula exists, so the general method is the companion matrix's eigenvalues -- and that whole chain lives in poly.zig over eigen_general.zig's Francis QR. This method binds arguments and marshals; it does not assemble a matrix and it does not decide anything.

methods.name: Times
methods.description: THE DOUBLE LOOP IS KEPT FOR SMALL DEGREES, and not out of caution: it is EXACT for integer coefficients, while the FFT route goes through irrational twiddle factors and comes back a few rounding errors away from a whole number. Below the crossover the direct method is both faster and more accurate, so preferring it is not a compromise. Above it, O(n log n) wins by enough that the rounding is worth paying.

methods.name: TimesViaTransform
methods.description: The same product through the frequency domain -- exposed so the guard can compare the two routes on the SAME polynomials rather than having to grow one past the crossover to reach this code.

methods.name: Block
methods.description: A limit SLOWS a key; a block STOPS it. A blocked key is refused by Allow() whether or not it has a limit -- an unconfigured key is otherwise unlimited, which is exactly the flood a responder must stop. Every refusal is recorded with the block's reason. A block made with BlockFor lifts by itself when its time is up; Block holds until Unblock.

methods.name: Allow
methods.description: the gate ----------------------------------------------------------- Try to admit ONE request for a key. An unconfigured key is UNLIMITED (always TRUE). A configured key takes a token: TRUE while the bucket has one, FALSE (rate limited) once spent, recovering as it refills.

methods.name: AllowN
methods.description: Admit n at once (all-or-nothing). Counts one allowed / one rejected DECISION regardless of n.

methods.name: Available

methods.name: WaitForAttributetoSettle

The settle state now lives ON THE OBJECT (aSettleWatchers records) and the timers go to the GLOBAL detached table, which every RunLoop drives. The lambda uses only its own params (oSelf!) -- the reason the watcher contract passes `this` first.

methods.name: Status
methods.description: The class recorded a status, a result and (now) an error, and offered no way to read any of them. A caller whose task failed could not ask what went wrong; a caller whose task succeeded could not collect the answer unless they had registered a handler first.

methods.name: WasReported
methods.description: Did the failure reach anyone -- a raise, a handler, or stdout? Only ERROR_IGNORE answers FALSE, and it is the one mode that asked to. Without this the fallback arm had no observable effect at all: removing it left every assertion green, because recording a reason is not reporting it.

methods.name: Complete
methods.description: Not every task computes. stzReactiveObject.SetAsync already HAS the value it is going to store, and its attempt to wrap one in a task function -- `func { return _newValue_ }` -- raised R24, because a Haro lambda cannot read a caller's local. These two let a caller that did the work itself still report it through the same task surface, so Status()/Result()/ Error() mean the same thing however the work happened.

methods.description: ── async TCP request/response ───────────────────────────

methods.description: Block up to nTimeoutMs for the response body (empty on error/timeout).

methods.name: SubmitSpawn
methods.description: Run a subprocess on the loop, capture its stdout, report the exit code -- non-Haro workers run OFF-THREAD, drained via the job idiom. The command is the program followed by its arguments. Submit; acArgv = [ program, arg1, arg2, ... ]. Returns a job id.

methods.name: AwaitSpawn
methods.description: Block up to nTimeoutMs for the child; returns its stdout.

methods.name: KillSpawn
methods.description: Force-kill a spawned child by job id: send nSignum (default SIGKILL=9; SIGTERM=15). On Windows libuv maps these to TerminateProcess. Returns 0 on success, negative on error (-2 not found, -3 already exited, -4 not a spawn / no handle). The kill is mutex-guarded in the engine so it can't race the loop thread reaping the process on its own exit.

methods.name: KillSpawnHard
methods.description: SIGKILL by default (the forceful stop for a wedged child).

methods.name: Spawn
methods.description: Submit + await in one call; returns the child's stdout.

methods.name: SubmitHttp
methods.description: A full HTTP(S) request runs on a libuv WORKER thread via curl (native Schannel TLS on Windows) and is drained through the job idiom -- so https:// is genuinely async, no TLS state machine on the loop. Methods: 0=GET 1=POST 2=PUT 3=DELETE 4=HEAD 5=OPTIONS 6=PATCH.

methods.name: HttpLastStatus
methods.description: HTTP status code of the last drained request (or < 0 on error).

methods.name: HttpGet
methods.description: Submit + await a GET in one call; returns the response body.

methods.name: HttpPost
methods.description: Submit + await a POST with a body; returns the response body.

methods.name: Listen
methods.description: A listener lives on the loop thread; Haro drains EVENTS: [ :accept, nConn, "" ] / [ :data, nConn, cBytes ] / [ :closed, nConn, "" ] / [] when there is none. In http mode each :data event is ONE complete framed HTTP/1.1 request (headers + Content-Length body, pipelining-safe). Raw TCP stream listener (IoT/telemetry). nPort 0 = ephemeral. Returns the server id (>0) or a negative uv error code.

methods.name: ListenHttp
methods.description: HTTP/1.1 listener: :data events carry complete requests.

methods.name: ListenStzm
methods.description: STZM message-plane listener (distribution D0): each :data event is ONE complete STZM frame (header + payload). Unpack with StzmUnpack().

methods.name: ListenStzmTls
methods.description: TLS-terminating STZM listener (D5): the same framed message plane over the same mbedTLS termination the HTTPS listener uses. A non-empty cCaPath verifies client certs; bRequireClient makes a valid one MANDATORY (mutual TLS node links).

methods.name: ConnectStzm
methods.description: Persistent CLIENT CHANNEL to a peer (distribution D0). The dial is async: the channel id comes back immediately; link-up arrives as an :accept event on ServerPoll/Await (a failed dial as :closed). The channel then speaks the SAME calls a listener does -- ServerWrite to send, ServerPoll to receive, ServerStop to hang up. A link is a link, whichever side dialed.

methods.name: ConnectRaw
methods.description: Raw-stream client channel (:data events carry stream chunks).

methods.name: ConnectStzmTls
methods.description: STZM channel over CLIENT-role TLS (the mTLS counterpart of ListenTls, on the persistent link): this node PRESENTS cCertPath/cKeyPath for the peer's mutual check ("" for none) and VALIDATES the peer -- see _TlsVerifyMode() for what bVerify may be. Link-up (:accept) fires only when the handshake COMPLETES -- an up channel is a SECURE channel.

methods.name: WaitLinkUp
methods.description: Block up to nTimeoutMs for the channel's link-up. Returns the conn id (> 0) to write on, or 0 (dial failed or timed out).

methods.name: ListenHttpTls
methods.description: TLS-terminating HTTP listener: each connection runs an mbedTLS handshake (server cert cCertPath + key cKeyPath) before the plaintext HTTP framing -- so the events Haro drains are DECRYPTED requests and ServerWrite responses are encrypted transparently. A non-empty cCaPath turns on client-cert verification; bRequireClient = TRUE makes a valid client cert MANDATORY (mutual TLS). Returns the server id (>0) or a negative error (TLS setup errors are -10..-17). Engine-terminated TLS.

methods.name: ListenHttpsServer
methods.description: One-way server TLS convenience (no client cert): serve HTTPS with just a server cert + key.

methods.name: TlsRequest
methods.description: Send cRequest (raw HTTP bytes) to cHost:nPort over TLS and return the response bytes ("" on failure -- see TlsClientStatus). This node PRESENTS the client cert cCertPath/cKeyPath (for the peer's mutual check; pass "" for none), and VALIDATES the peer's server cert (hostname checked via SNI) -- see _TlsVerifyMode() for bVerify. A dedicated mbedTLS transport (PEM certs + mutual auth), separate from the curl path used for general outbound HTTPS.

methods.name: TlsGet
methods.description: Convenience: build + send a GET over TLS. Same cert/verify semantics.

methods.name: TlsClientStatus
methods.description: Result of the last TlsRequest: 0 ok, -1 connect, -2 handshake (an untrusted/invalid peer SERVER cert aborts here), -3 cert verify, -4 setup, -18 verification switched off without :InsecureNoVerify, -19 no trust anchor. NOTE: a server rejecting a MISSING client cert is enforced SERVER-side -- under TLS 1.3 the client's handshake still completes (status 0) but the protected response comes back EMPTY. So the authoritative "was I let in?" check is the RESPONSE body, not status.

methods.name: ServerPort
methods.description: Actual bound port (useful after nPort = 0).

methods.name: ServerConns
methods.description: tls client (the mtls counterpart to listenhttptls)

methods.name: ServerPoll
methods.description: Drain one event without blocking; [] if none.

methods.name: ServerAwait
methods.description: Block up to nTimeoutMs for one event; [] on timeout.

methods.name: ServerWrite
methods.description: Write to a connection; bCloseAfter closes it once the write lands.

methods.name: ServerCloseConn
methods.description: tls client (the mtls counterpart to listenhttptls)

methods.name: ServerSetInbox
methods.description: Bounded inbox (distribution D1): cap the QUEUED data events with a declared overflow policy -- :DropOldest / :DropNewest / :Refuse (reject and hang up, so the sender observes it). nCap 0 = unbounded. Overflow is COUNTED (ServerOverflow), never silent.

methods.description: the PORT contract, same three arguments as the sandbox

methods.name: FetchAll
methods.description: Submit a whole batch across the loops (so they run concurrently), then await each. aRequests is a list of [cHost, nPort, cPayload]. Returns a list of response bodies (same order as the input).

methods.name: init
methods.description: @aParentStack / @nParentIndex lived here to track parents during a declarative setup that was replaced: nothing ever pushed to the stack, so the index it derived was always 0, and nothing read it either. AddChildLevel() finds a parent BY NAME (pvtFindLevelByName).

methods.name: RefinementPoints
methods.description: the declared change surface

methods.name: Cascade
methods.description: CASCADE: the pre-commit blast radius (the review artifact) ----------- which source LINES the point sits on, plus any point that shares a line (the floor's cross-point impact). "What you read instead of the diff" (5.8).

methods.name: DeclareDerivation
methods.description: STAGE 3 wiring: cross-point DERIVATION rules ------------------------ A derivation rule is a named predicate over the code's POST-change state: fPredicate(oCode) returns TRUE when the state is consistent. It fires AFTER the value is tentatively applied and rolls the change back if any rule rejects (so cross-point invariants -- "vat cannot exceed the ceiling", "heap needs a threshold" -- are enforceable). Same {name, function, message} record shape as stzGraphRule.

methods.name: GovernedBy
methods.description: STAGE 4 wiring: GOVERNANCE (refining is a governed action) ---------- Wire a (fully configured) stzGovernance. Each point's refinement is the action "refine-<point>"; To() calls MayProceed(actor, action) so a refinement needs permission (CAN) + authority (SHOULD) covering the point's declared risk tier before it can mutate the source. the NAME of the object that governs this code ("" if none)

methods.name: Actor
methods.description: the actor this code acts as

methods.name: As
methods.description: EXECUTION TRUST POSTURES (5.8) -------------------------------------- A posture says WHERE a refinement came from. Trust rank (high -> low): :trusted (3, in-process/verified) > :external (2, an external tool) > :sandboxed (1, isolated run) > :llm (0, LLM-composed). A proposal defaults to :trusted; As(posture) declares otherwise for the next To(). The posture rides into the audit chain; a point's TrustFloor refuses anything below the required rank (LLM-composed edits to a critical knob can be forbidden without forbidding a human's).

methods.name: SetRiskFor
methods.description: Governance config MUST go through these delegators: GovernedBy stores a COPY (governance is pure Haro lists, no shared handle), so mutating the caller's original would leave this copy stale (the Haro aliasing doctrine). Delegating keeps @oGov the one live truth. Declare a point's refinement risk tier ("refine-<point>").

methods.name: SetAllowRefine
methods.description: Grant the actor permission (CAN) to refine a point.

methods.name: SetAuthorityLevel
methods.description: Set the actor's authority (SHOULD): :Advisory/:Delegated/ :Autonomous/:EmergencyOverride.

methods.name: GovernanceQ
methods.description: The wired governance as a chainable object (Q-convention) -- returns a fresh copy each call; use for READS (Why/Lineage/NumberOfDecisions).

methods.name: Refine
methods.description: the typed proposal + the gate

methods.name: To
methods.description: apply a value to the pending point THROUGH the gate. Returns [ :admitted, :why ]; on rejection the source is unchanged.

methods.name: CanRevert
methods.description: reversibility (a data-model primitive)

methods.name: Revert
methods.description: undo the last admitted refinement -- a TYPED inverse (single step).

methods.name: RevertTo
methods.description: ATOMIC multi-step revert: roll the source back to exactly nStep applied refinements (0 = the original source), undoing each step in reverse via its typed inverse. Every undone step is pushed onto the REDO stack. This is reversibility as a data-model primitive: time-travel over the timeline, not a one-off undo button.

methods.name: Redo
methods.description: RE-APPLY the most recently reverted step (undo the undo). A fresh admitted Refine clears the redo stack (the timeline forked).

methods.name: Checkpoint
methods.description: A named marker on the timeline; RevertToCheckpoint rewinds to it.

methods.name: History
methods.description: The ordered applied timeline: [ name, old, new, posture ] per step.

methods.name: PostureOf
methods.description: The posture recorded for a given applied step (1-based; "" if none).

methods.name: Rendered
methods.description: rendering ------------------------------------------------------------ the source with every point's CURRENT value in place (the R-tags stay -- the point is a living knob, not a one-shot substitution)

methods.name: CallEdges
methods.description: Haro-specific call queries (a class-qualified 3-tuple model)

methods.name: RawCallEntries
methods.description: The UNRESOLVED call targets, [ class, method, callee, line ] -- every identifier called in a method body, builtins included. CallEdges() keeps only calls to DEFINED methods (so it drops builtins like substr); a rule like engine-first needs to SEE the builtin calls, so it reads these. The line is the CALL SITE, and a `def substr(` is a definition (not harvested here), so this distinguishes a call from a definition -- which a text scan of "substr(" cannot.

methods.name: CallersOf

methods.name: CalleesOf

methods.name: DeadCode
methods.description: DEAD CODE (honest scope): PRIVATE helpers (name starts "_") whose name is never referenced by any call in the scanned tree. Public methods are excluded -- they may be entry points called from outside this tree.

methods.name: CyclicCalls
methods.description: CYCLIC CALLS (honest scope): intra-class MUTUAL RECURSION -- method A and B in the same class each call the other (a 2-cycle). Self-recursion (A calls A) is legitimate and not reported. Name-based within one class.

methods.name: AddCase
methods.description: A PICTURE THE RULES ARE JUDGED AGAINST. It must already be rendered: every plastic rule reads render facts, and a diagram that has not been drawn answers with empty lists -- which would read as an empty scope and convict every rule in the set of being dead. THE CASE a rule set is judged against -- a rendered picture for the graph plane, a code graph for stzCodeRule, an agent graph, an org chart. The governance never asks what kind it is; it asks the RULES what they govern in it, which is the only thing that has to be domain-specific.

methods.name: AddPicture
methods.description: A PICTURE IS SOLVED BEFORE IT IS COPIED. Haro copies an object into a list, and a copy of an unsolved picture solves itself again the first time a scope asks it anything -- so a corpus of 52 unsolved pictures paid 52 layouts at its first question, 26 seconds of the gate's governor, and the caller's own picture paid the same again when it was asked. Solved here, in the caller's hand (a parameter is a reference), the copy carries the solution and every later copy of the caller's picture does too.

methods.name: DeclarePrecedence
methods.description: A DECLARED PRECEDENCE between two rules that reach for one subject. The reason is required: a precedence without one is a coin toss that somebody will later reverse in good faith.

methods.name: CheckPictures
methods.description: the rules against the pictures ----------------------------------- What the rules say about the corpus -- the ordinary half, kept here so one call answers both halves and neither can be run without the other being available.

methods.name: CheckRules
methods.description: the rules against themselves ------------------------------------- The five questions. Every finding here is about a RULE, so :where is the rule's name and the corpus is the evidence, which is the inverse of CheckPictures and the reason both exist.

methods.name: CheckAll
methods.description: both halves, and the verdict -------------------------------------- Everything: what the rules say about the pictures, and what the governor says about the rules.

methods.name: ScopeTable
methods.description: How much of the corpus each rule actually governs -- the number that turns "is this scope right" from an opinion into a reading.

methods.name: Run
methods.description: collecting findings --------------------------------------------- Run a rule set over a graph and collect its findings (already unified, carrying :subject from each rule's domain).

methods.name: Collect
methods.description: Collect a GRAPH's own findings -- the graph checks ITSELF (CheckRules) and the report ingests. This is the Softanza-oriented gate: each graph owns its rules and reports itself; the report just gathers them across domains. oRep.Collect(oCodeGraph).Collect(oAgentGraph).Collect(oSecurityGraph) Any object answering CheckRules() qualifies (stzGraph, stzAgentGraph, stzSecurityGraph, stzOrgChart, stzCodeGraph).

methods.name: SetClaimCheck

methods.name: SetUniversal

methods.description: SAFE reads (never leak the value)

methods.name: SourceLocator
methods.description: the POINTER to where the secret lives -- an env var NAME, a file PATH, a vault REF. Safe to show: it is not the secret. (For :literal it is "(inline)", never the value.)

methods.name: Descriptor
methods.description: the redacted, safe representation used EVERYWHERE the secret is displayed or serialised. No value ever appears here.

methods.name: IsRevealableBy
methods.description: the GOVERNED reveal -- the ONLY path to plaintext ---------------- may this actor read the plaintext? Only an effectful, non-sandboxed actor.

methods.name: Reveal
methods.description: resolve + return the plaintext -- GATED. An LLMActor (inference-only) is refused; a HumanActor (effectful, trusted) succeeds. A vault-sourced secret needs a resolver (see RevealVia).

methods.name: RevealFor
methods.description: Same as Reveal: resolve + return the plaintext -- GATED. An LLMActor (inference-only) is refused; a HumanActor (effectful, trusted) succeeds. A vault-sourced secret needs a resolver (see RevealVia).

methods.name: RevealVia
methods.description: resolver-aware reveal: a vault-sourced secret is fetched THROUGH a resolver, passed by reference at reveal time (after the actor gate). ANY object with a Resolve(locator) method is a valid resolver -- your vault client, or the reference stzVaultResolver. For a non-vault secret the resolver is ignored and this behaves like Reveal(actor).

methods.name: IsResolvableBy
methods.description: does the secret resolve to a non-empty value? Governed. A vault-sourced secret needs a resolver, so it is not resolvable this way.

methods.name: Register
methods.description: the registry ----------------------------------------------------- register a secret under its own Name(). Registering a name that exists REPLACES it -- that is rotation (RotateQ is the explicit alias).

methods.name: Rotate
methods.description: rotate a secret: replace whatever is registered under poNewSecret's name.

methods.name: RotateToFresh
methods.description: ROTATE IN PLACE, to a fresh random value -- containment's :RotateSecret. Only a secret whose value THIS store holds (a :literal) can be regenerated here: a key it issues, a token it signs with. A secret that lives in an environment variable, a file or a vault is not this store's to change -- that REFUSES loudly, naming where to rotate it, rather than pretending. Creating a credential is an effect, so poActor passes the same gate as a reveal. The new value is 32 random bytes as 64 hex characters; kind and name are kept (a token's expiry is cleared -- a new value is a new credential). Returns This.

methods.name: Revoke
methods.description: revoke (remove) a secret by name.

methods.name: Has
methods.description: safe reads (never leak a value)

methods.name: Names
methods.description: the project's whole credential surface, by name -- safe to show/log.

methods.name: Secret
methods.description: the secret OBJECT (still self-redacting -- holding it does not reveal it).

methods.name: DescriptorOf
methods.description: the redacted descriptor of a registered secret (never its value).

methods.name: Reveal
methods.description: the ONE governed door to a value (gate + audit) ----------------- reveal a secret's plaintext -- GATED (only an effectful, non-sandboxed actor) and AUDITED (the access is recorded either way). This is the only path a value leaves the store, so the log is complete.

methods.name: RevealVia
methods.description: reveal through a vault RESOLVER (for a :vault-sourced secret), still gated and AUDITED by the store. For a non-vault secret the resolver is ignored, so this is a safe superset of Reveal.

methods.name: IsRevealableBy
methods.description: may this actor reveal this secret? (no side effect, no audit entry.)

methods.name: SaveSealedTo
methods.description: Write the whole store to pcPath as ONE authenticated-encryption blob (XChaCha20-Poly1305), keyed by poKeySecret -- itself a stzSecret, whose 64-hex value comes from wherever secrets come from (an environment variable, a file, a vault). Literal values are sealed; env / file / vault secrets are saved as their POINTER only -- the plaintext never leaves its source. The store's name is bound as the aad, so one store's file cannot be passed off as another's. Sealing reads every literal value, so poActor passes the same gate as a reveal.

methods.name: SaveSealedToVia
methods.description: As SaveSealedTo, with the KEY fetched through a vault resolver (R4).

methods.name: RefusedAccesses
methods.description: refused reveals -- a misuse signal worth watching.

methods.name: RotateSecret
methods.description: the target is the secret's NAME, as the incident names it

methods.name: MayAttest
methods.description: the governed export ------------------------------------------ Reading the evidence out is a SENSING act -- an inference-only actor may not perform it.

methods.name: WriteTo
methods.description: Seal the ledger to a file, attested by this actor. Returns TRUE when written; FALSE (with the refusal recorded) when the actor may not.

methods.name: Statement
methods.description: the custody statement ---------------------------------------- What a person (or an auditor) reads beside the file.

methods.name: SpawnTarget
methods.description: the target ---------------------------------------------------- Spawn the application under attack: a real stzAppServer child with an open ledger, a real stzAuth, and a real signed-request gate.

methods.name: FireCredentialStuffing
methods.description: the attacks --------------------------------------------------- Guess a password until the account's failure counter says so.

methods.name: FireForgery
methods.description: Present a signature that does not verify.

methods.name: FireReplay
methods.description: Send a VALID signed request twice -- the second is a replay.

methods.name: CollectEvidence
methods.description: acquisition: evidence crosses the boundary -------------------- Ask the target to seal its ledger, then VERIFY the file and rebuild a working ledger from it. The parent believes nothing it has not verified.

methods.name: OpenVictimSession
methods.description: containment: the loop closes ---------------------------------- Log the victim in for real BEFORE the attack, so containment has a live session to end and the drill can prove it ended.

methods.name: Contain
methods.description: Contain what the evidence shows, as poOperator. The plan is derived FROM THE ACQUIRED EVIDENCE (an incident per credential-stuffing finding), governed HERE -- MayCommit is judged on the operator, and an LLM actor is refused -- and carried to the target, whose REAL responder (stzAuthResponder over its own stzAuth) performs it. Then containment is VERIFIED from outside: the right password must now be refused, and the session opened before the attack must be dead. Returns the number of actions committed.

methods.name: ContainmentHolds
methods.description: Verified from outside the target: the correct password is refused, and the pre-attack session no longer answers.

methods.name: TimeToDetectMs
methods.description: The two numbers a drill exists to produce, in milliseconds of wall time: from the first attack sent to the evidence showing every expected detection, and from there to containment applied and verified. -1 when that point was never reached.

methods.name: Passed
methods.description: Did every expected detection actually fire?

methods.description: legibility

methods.name: Kind
methods.description: reads

methods.name: IsRefusal
methods.description: "granted" and "observed" are not refusals; "refused" and "failed" are. Written as an explicit list rather than `!= "granted"` because a fourth outcome arrived later (see Observed) and the negative form would have silently swept it in -- an expired session would have counted as a refusal in every pivot.

methods.name: ByActor
methods.description: building (fluent; every setter returns This) --------------- WHO: an stzSystemActor contributes its own facts -- name, posture, capability kinds. Nothing is invented here.

methods.name: ByActorNamed
methods.description: For a caller with no actor object yet (an unauthenticated request, a username at the login door).

methods.name: About
methods.description: WHICH thing. THE REDACTION LAW lives here: an object contributes its DESCRIPTOR (stzSecret.Descriptor() is the redacted form), never its value -- this class never calls Reveal(). A string is taken as already-safe; callers pass descriptors like "user:admin", "key:billing", "route:/pay".

methods.name: OccurredAt
methods.description: The deterministic form (the house "...At(now)" convention): an event that did not happen NOW carries its own wall clock -- a replayed or imported record, or a guard that needs exact window arithmetic instead of machine speed. The monotonic stamp is left alone: it orders THIS process's events and cannot be borrowed.

methods.name: Granted
methods.description: outcomes

methods.name: Failed
methods.description: The gate admitted it and the act still did not complete.

methods.name: Observed
methods.description: NOT A VERDICT -- something simply happened (incident I2's session seams). A session reaching its expiry was neither granted nor refused: no gate ran, nobody was told no. Forcing such a fact into "refused" would have made every pivot that counts refusals over-count, and would have taught an investigator that routine housekeeping was an attack. The ledger's job is to witness, and some of what it witnesses carries no judgment at all.

methods.name: AsInfo

methods.name: Record
methods.description: the native record

methods.name: CanonicalString
methods.description: The separator is reserved: a field's own pipes fold to "/" so the ledger can split the line back into fields without a field's content (a reason quoting a message, say) shifting every field after it. Sanitizing at the source beats parsing bravely later.

methods.name: OcsfSeverityId
methods.description: interop: OCSF (the SIEM schema) ---------------------------- OCSF severity_id: 1 Informational, 3 Medium, 4 High.

methods.name: OcsfStatusId
methods.description: OCSF status_id: 1 Success, 2 Failure.

methods.name: OcsfClassUid
methods.description: Best-effort class mapping, honestly bounded: auth/sso/oauth are Identity & Access Management (category 3, class 3002 Authentication); http.* is Network Activity (4 / 4002 HTTP Activity); everything else is Application Activity (6 / 6003 API Activity). Facts that do not map cleanly ride in "unmapped", which is what that OCSF field is for.

methods.name: Uses

methods.description: a secret lives in a store

methods.name: MayAttach
methods.description: the CONSTRAINT: no live secret to a sandboxed actor ------------- TRUE when attaching pcSecret to pcActor keeps the surface sound (a sandboxed actor must not hold a live secret it could exfiltrate).

methods.name: AttachSecret
methods.description: Attach a secret to an actor -- the governed door. REFUSED for a sandboxed actor at construction (audit -> gate), so the escalation can never enter the graph through the sanctioned API.

methods.name: ReachesEffectful
methods.description: queries --------------------------------------------------------- Can this actor reach the 'effectful' capability by ANY path (directly, or through a tool, or through delegation)? The multi-hop escalation question.

methods.name: PathToCapability
methods.description: THE PATH ITSELF, not merely whether one exists (incident I5): an investigation must be able to say HOW an actor could reach a capability -- "billing-agent -> deploy-tool -> effectful" -- and an empty list means no path.

methods.name: CutCapability
methods.description: Remove EVERY path by which pcActor reaches pcCapability, by cutting the actor's OWN first-hop edges that lead there: a capability it holds directly, a tool it uses that grants it, an actor it delegates to that reaches it. Other actors are untouched -- a colleague using the same tool keeps it. Returns the edges removed, as [ from, label, to ].

methods.name: Capacity
methods.description: The engine's own answer -- a face bound to the process ledger (AdoptHandle) never knew the capacity it was created with.

methods.name: Record
methods.description: recording --------------------------------------------------- Append an stzSecurityEvent. The engine chains it; nothing about the digest is under the caller's control.

methods.name: AppendCanonical
methods.description: Append a canonical line directly -- the acquisition path (I8), used when rebuilding a ledger from verified evidence. The chain is recomputed here; it does not carry the original file's.

methods.name: PersistTo
methods.description: Call it BEFORE recording. Returns [ :ok, :verified, :brokenAt, :why ]; a broken stored history is REFUSED (:ok = 0) and nothing is attached.

methods.name: VerifyDurable
methods.description: Verify the WHOLE stored history from genesis -- where Verify() can only speak for the retained window. [ :intact, :brokenAt, :message ]

methods.description: Events ever recorded (keeps counting past capacity).

methods.name: Size

methods.name: At
methods.description: reading ----------------------------------------------------- The record at 1-based position i (oldest retained first), in the I0 field shape plus its chain digest.

methods.name: OfActor
methods.description: the analyst's pivots

methods.name: Refusals
methods.description: Everything that was not granted -- the signal to watch. Refused and failed -- NOT "everything that is not granted". The negative form was here too, and it was wrong the moment the OBSERVED outcome arrived (I2's session seams): an expired session would have been counted as a refusal by this pivot, in a system whose whole point is that a warning must mean something. Kept in step with stzSecurityEvent.IsRefusal(), deliberately as one positive list.

methods.name: Digest
methods.description: the chain --------------------------------------------------- The head digest: one string that commits to the ENTIRE history ever recorded (including evicted entries).

methods.name: Verify
methods.description: [ :intact, :brokenAt, :message ] -- brokenAt is the 1-based index of the first entry whose stored digest disagrees with a recomputation, 0 when the retained window is consistent.

methods.name: SealAttestedTo
methods.description: sealing (evidence leaves the process) ----------------------- Write the retained window as a verifiable file: one "<digest>TAB<canonical>" line per entry, a header carrying the count and an HMAC seal over (head digest | count). Re-check it with StzVerifySealedLedger(path, key) -- editing any line breaks the chain; editing the seal without the key is not possible. As SealTo, plus WHO attested and WHEN -- the custody header that turns a sealed file into an attested one (I7). Unknown "#" lines are ignored by verifiers, so the format stayed compatible.

Two engines, unified: (1) the GRAMMAR composes a method name from the intent and grounds it against this class's real API; if the class implements it, that is the answer (highest confidence, it is derived not guessed). (2) Otherwise fall back to semantic RETRIEVAL (the ranker: reranker/embeddings/lexical). Returns a human line: the call template + how it was resolved + the name's grammatical gloss.

methods.name: Declare
methods.description: the dependency surface ------------------------------------------- Declare a service this solution depends on, before anything is bound. This is what turns "what does this touch?" from archaeology into a query -- and it is what lets an UNBOUND dependency be a finding rather than a surprise.

methods.name: Bind
methods.description: binding ---------------------------------------------------------- Bind an implementation. The posture is asked OF THE OBJECT: anything with IsSandbox() answering true is a sandbox. Declaring itself beats guessing from a class name, and it means a third-party double can opt in.

methods.name: BindSandbox
methods.description: ...say it explicitly when the object cannot.

methods.name: BindLocal
methods.description: Bind a genuine LOCAL equivalent -- sqlite, the filesystem, a local model. Not a fake, so unlike a sandbox this may ship; see the posture note above.

methods.name: BindLive
methods.description: Bind the real thing, naming the STORE SECRET its credential lives in. The name, not the key: a registry that held credentials would be one more place they leak from.

methods.name: Unbind
methods.description: Remove the IMPLEMENTATION but keep the dependency. The service is then declared-and-unbound, which IS a finding -- your solution still needs the thing, it just has nothing to serve it. To retire the dependency itself, use Undeclare.

methods.name: Undeclare
methods.description: Retire the dependency altogether -- the solution no longer needs this service. Unbinds it too, so nothing is left half-declared.

methods.name: Service
methods.description: resolution (what the application actually calls) ------------------ The service by name. RAISES when nothing is bound -- an unbound dependency that silently returned NULL would fail later, somewhere else, as a null-call with no hint of the real cause.

methods.name: SandboxedServices
methods.description: every service still bound to a fake -- the "what is not real yet" list.

methods.name: LocalServices
methods.description: the genuinely-local ones: real, self-hosted, shippable.

methods.name: SetPhase
methods.description: the phase -------------------------------------------------------- :development / :emulated -> sandboxes are expected. :production -> they are a violation. The phase is the SAME switch stzDelivery already uses, so nothing new decides what is real.

methods.name: FindingsVia
methods.description: governance ------------------------------------------------------- [ [ :invariant, :severity, :where, :message ], ... ] -- the same shape stzSecurityPosture and the graph rules use, so one CI gate covers all three. poStore may be NULL when there is no keyring to check against. NOTE: each _Check returns its OWN list and this LOOPS to append the elements. Haro's `+` on a list appends the whole list as ONE element, so `_aF_ + This._Check...()` would nest rather than accumulate -- and a nested findings list silently reports zero errors. Same shape as stzSecurityPosture.

methods.name: MayGoLive
methods.description: ASKED IN THE PRODUCTION FRAME, whatever the current phase. "May I go LIVE?" IS the production question, so answering it from a :development phase would have said YES with a fake still bound -- the phase-dependent invariants (sandbox-in-production, ephemeral-in-production) simply had not fired yet. The phase is set, the surface judged, the phase restored: asking is not declaring. (Found while writing the narration; the guard had only ever asked after setting production, so the honest answer and the convenient one agreed.)

methods.name: FindingsForProductionVia
methods.description: the surface judged as production would judge it, then put back

methods.name: WhyNotLive
methods.description: ...and the same, but explaining itself.

methods.name: AsRuleGraph
methods.description: NOTE this does NOT duplicate the invariants above. Findings from Findings() already carry the report's shape, so the registry joins the shared CI gate directly:  oReport.IngestLegacy(oReg.Findings(), "services"). What the GRAPH adds is the question a flag check cannot ask -- which PART of a solution depends on a fake -- and that needs the delivery's parts joined to these nodes (see stzDelivery.AsRuleGraph and stzServiceRuleSet).

methods.description: THE BILL. A test can assert it, exactly as the LLM port lets you assert tokens.
